quests.sentence: This laptop is faster than my old one.
quests.ruleExplanation: Faster adds -er to fast for a short adjective, and than introduces the second item being compared, my old one.
quests.nativeTip: Add -er to a short adjective, then use than to introduce what it's being compared to.

quests.sentence: Her apartment is more spacious than mine.
quests.ruleExplanation: More spacious uses more before a longer adjective instead of adding -er, followed by than and mine.
quests.nativeTip: Longer adjectives use more instead of -er, still followed by than and the second item.

quests.sentence: He is taller than his brother.
quests.ruleExplanation: Taller adds -er to a short adjective, and than his brother names who he's being compared to.
quests.nativeTip: The short-adjective plus -er pattern still applies, then than introduces the comparison.

quests.sentence: This is the fastest route to downtown.
quests.ruleExplanation: The fastest uses the plus -est to single out one item as the best in its category among all others, followed by route to downtown.
quests.nativeTip: Use the before a superlative, and add -est to a short adjective to compare against everything else.

quests.sentence: She is the most experienced candidate.
quests.ruleExplanation: The most experienced uses the most before a longer adjective, singling out one candidate as the top among all others.
quests.nativeTip: Longer adjectives use the most instead of -est, still preceded by the.

quests.sentence: That was the best decision we made.
quests.ruleExplanation: The best decision uses the irregular superlative best (not gooder or goodest), following the same the-plus-superlative pattern.
quests.nativeTip: The plus a short irregular superlative like best still leads into the noun it describes.

quests.sentence: This test is as difficult as the last one.
quests.ruleExplanation: As difficult as sandwiches the adjective difficult between two as words, showing this test and the last one are equally hard.
quests.nativeTip: As...as sandwiches the adjective between two as words, comparing two things as equal.

quests.sentence: She runs as fast as her teammates.
quests.ruleExplanation: As fast as sandwiches fast between the two as words, comparing her running speed equally to her teammates'.
quests.nativeTip: The same as...as pattern compares two things as equally fast, not one faster than the other.

quests.sentence: The new model isn't as reliable as the old one.
quests.ruleExplanation: Isn't as reliable as shows the new model falls short of the old one's reliability — negating as...as expresses inequality, not equality.
quests.nativeTip: A negative before as...as shows the two things are NOT equal, the opposite of the previous two sentences.

quests.sentence: This coffee is too hot to drink.
quests.ruleExplanation: Too hot to drink shows the coffee's temperature is excessive, making the action to drink impossible or unpleasant.
quests.nativeTip: Too plus an adjective, then to plus the base verb, shows something is excessive for that action.

quests.sentence: The instructions are too complicated to follow.
quests.ruleExplanation: Too complicated to follow shows the instructions exceed a reasonable level of difficulty for the action of following them.
quests.nativeTip: The same too-plus-adjective-plus-infinitive pattern shows the instructions are excessively hard to follow.

quests.sentence: She is too busy to answer calls.
quests.ruleExplanation: Too busy to answer shows her schedule is excessively full, preventing the action of answering calls.
quests.nativeTip: Too still shows excess, this time making an action (answering calls) impossible.

quests.sentence: He is old enough to drive.
quests.ruleExplanation: Old enough to drive places enough after the adjective old, showing a sufficient level has been reached for the action to drive.
quests.nativeTip: Enough comes after the adjective (not before, like too), then to plus the base verb.

quests.sentence: The room isn't big enough for everyone.
quests.ruleExplanation: Isn't big enough shows the room falls short of a sufficient size, with for everyone naming who it's insufficient for.
quests.nativeTip: A negative before adjective-plus-enough shows the level is insufficient, not excessive like too.

quests.sentence: She is qualified enough to lead the project.
quests.ruleExplanation: Qualified enough to lead places enough right after qualified, showing she has reached a sufficient level for the action to lead the project.
quests.nativeTip: Enough still follows the adjective directly, before the infinitive phrase.

quests.sentence: How much time do you need?
quests.ruleExplanation: How much time asks about an uncountable quantity, since time cannot be counted individually, followed by do you need in question order.
quests.nativeTip: How much asks about an uncountable noun like time, and stays together as one question phrase.

quests.sentence: How many employees work here?
quests.ruleExplanation: How many employees asks about a countable noun (since employees can be counted one by one), unlike how much for uncountable nouns.
quests.nativeTip: How many asks about a countable noun like employees, a different question word from how much.

quests.sentence: We don't have much information yet.
quests.ruleExplanation: Don't have much information uses much before the uncountable noun information, showing this pairing works in negative statements as well as questions.
quests.nativeTip: Much pairs with an uncountable noun in a negative statement too, not just in questions.

quests.sentence: She has a few close friends.
quests.ruleExplanation: A few close friends expresses a positive view of the quantity, suggesting a small but satisfying number of friends.
quests.nativeTip: A few (with 'a') gives a positive feeling — some, and that's enough.

quests.sentence: Few people attended the seminar.
quests.ruleExplanation: Few people (without a) expresses a negative view of the turnout, suggesting an insufficient number attended — contrast this with a few in the previous sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Few without 'a' gives a negative feeling — almost none, not enough.

quests.sentence: We have little time to prepare.
quests.ruleExplanation: Little time (without a) expresses a negative view, suggesting there isn't enough time to prepare — the uncountable counterpart to few.
quests.nativeTip: Little without 'a' works the same negative way for uncountable nouns, meaning almost none.

quests.sentence: Each participant received a certificate.
quests.ruleExplanation: Each participant treats every member of the group one by one, taking a singular noun and singular verb received.
quests.nativeTip: Each treats members of a group individually, taking a singular noun and singular verb.

quests.sentence: Both candidates answered the questions well.
quests.ruleExplanation: Both candidates refers to exactly two people together, taking the plural verb answered, unlike each which treats members one by one.
quests.nativeTip: Both refers to exactly two people or things together, taking a plural verb.

quests.sentence: Every department submitted its report.
quests.ruleExplanation: Every department views the whole set of departments collectively, but like each, still takes a singular noun and verb submitted.
quests.nativeTip: Every views the whole group as a set, still taking a singular noun and verb like each.

quests.sentence: Either option works for me.
quests.ruleExplanation: Either option refers to one of exactly two choices, taking the singular verb works.
quests.nativeTip: Either refers to one of two options, in a positive statement, taking a singular verb.

quests.sentence: Neither candidate accepted the offer.
quests.ruleExplanation: Neither candidate means not one of the two candidates, carrying its own built-in negative meaning without needing a separate not.
quests.nativeTip: Neither refers to not one of two options, and it's already negative — no extra 'not' needed.

quests.sentence: You can choose either color.
quests.ruleExplanation: Either color offers a choice between exactly two options, following can choose in the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Either still refers to one of two, this time inside a can-statement about choice.

quests.sentence: Neither model is fast enough for our needs.
quests.ruleExplanation: Neither model states that not one of the two options qualifies, and fast enough for our needs explains exactly how they fall short.
quests.nativeTip: Combine neither (not one of two) with adjective-plus-enough for insufficient degree.

quests.sentence: Both candidates were more qualified than expected.
quests.ruleExplanation: Both candidates refers to the pair together, and were more qualified than expected uses a comparative to describe how they exceeded expectations.
quests.nativeTip: Combine both (referring to the pair together) with a comparative structure.

quests.sentence: We don't have enough time to finish every task.
quests.ruleExplanation: Don't have enough time states an insufficient amount, and to finish every task names the individualized goal (every, one by one) that falls short of that time.
quests.nativeTip: Combine a negative enough-statement with every, reviewing two quantity skills from this file.
